newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says HK will suffer if China denied trade.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says HK will suffer if China denied trade.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Saturday that Hong Kong's economy would be badly shaken if the United States failed to extend Most Favored Nation trading status to China.

Anticipating a fight with Congress on the issue, Clinton used his weekly radio address to argue why the United States should for another year give favorable tariff treatment to Chinese exports to America.

He said Hong Kong handled more than half the trade between the United States and China, making the British colony acutely sensitive to any disruption as it prepares to revert to Chinese rule on July 1.
"One thing we must not do is take any measures that would weaken Hong Kong just when it most needs to be strong and free," Clinton said.
He said a disruption would cut Hong Kong's economic growth in half, double unemployment by eliminating 85,000 jobs and reduce its trade by as much as $32 billion.

The White House released a supportive letter written by former Treasury Secretary William Simon and signed by nine other living former treasury secretaries, including Republicans such as James Baker and George Schultz and Clinton's first treasury secretary Lloyd Bentsen.
"Severing our trade with China will succeed only in isolating the United States, not in isolating China," the letter said.

Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten also had a letter to Clinton released by the White House in which he argued against anything but unconditional renewal of Most Favored Nation status for China for a full year.
"Unconditional renewal of China's MFN status for a full year is the most valuable single gift that the United States can present to Hong Kong during the handover period," Patten wrote.

A vote in Congress is expected later this month. Congress could vote to overturn Clinton's decision but would need to muster a two-thirds majority to make its action stick in the face of a presidential veto.
Conservative Republican Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has introduced a resolution in the Senate to deny MFN to China.
House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri has said he would oppose extending MFN to China in the House of Representatives.

Clinton and his top aides have waged a high-profile campaign to convince Congress to let China keep the trading status, arguing that remaining engaged with Beijing offers the best opportunity for bringing about democratic reforms, human rights improvements and opening markets in China.

"Hong Kong's leaders, present and future, understand the stakes involved," Clinton said. "They want to maintain their freedom and their autonomy. They know they need normal trading status to do it," Clinton said.

Clinton also promised that once the handover occurred, the United States would "keep a close watch on the transition process and the preservation of freedoms that the people of Hong Kong have relied on to build a prosperous, dynamic society."
